Then He mentioned the attribute of "the most pious": ﴿who gives his wealth﴾, that is, he gives it and spends it in the ways of good. The phrase *yatazakkā* (يتزكى) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the subject of *yu'ti* (يؤتي), meaning: while he seeks to be pure before Allah, not seeking to show off or to be heard of. It may also be a substitute (*badal*) for *yu'ti*, being included with it within the relative clause.

The majority recited *yatazakkā*, the imperfect of *tazakkā*. 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Ali recited *yazzakkā* (يزكى), with the *tā'* assimilated into the *zāy*.

﴿And for no one has he a favor to be repaid﴾: this sentence is independent, confirming what precedes it, that the purification is sincere and free from anything that contradicts sincerity. That is, he is not one who gives his wealth in order to be repaid by someone's favor done to him, or to reward that person for it. Rather, he seeks by his charity the face of Allah, the Most High. The meaning is that there is no one among the people who has a favor upon him that deserves to be repaid, such that he intends by his giving to repay it. *Tujzā* (تجزى) was said in the imperfect passive for the sake of the rhyme of the verses; the original would be *yajziyuhā iyyāhu* (يجزيها إياه) or *yajziyuhu iyyāhā* (يجزيه إياها).

﴿Except seeking the face of his Lord, the Most High﴾: the majority recited *ibtighā'* (ابتغاء) in the accusative. It may be accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*, the object expressing the reason for the action), meaning: he gives only seeking the face of his Lord, the Most High. It may also be accusative as an object according to an interpretation, meaning: "I did not give you seeking your recompense, but seeking the face of Allah." Yahya ibn Wathhab recited it in the nominative, as a substitute (*badal*) for the position of *ni'mah* (نعمة), since its position is nominative either as subject or as the beginning of a sentence, and *min* (من) is extra. The nominative is the dialect of Tamim, for they permit substitution in the disconnected (exceptive) construction and treat it like the connected one.

Makki said: al-Farra' permitted the nominative of *ibtighā'* as a substitute for the position of *ni'mah*, but this is far-fetched.

Shihab al-Din said: it seems he (Makki) was unaware of it as a recitation. His regarding it as far-fetched is itself far-fetched, for it is a widespread dialect. The majority also recited *ibtighā'* with the long vowel, while Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited it with the short vowel (*qasr*).

*Al-A'lā* (الأعلى) is an adjective (*na't*) describing the Lord.

﴿And he will surely be pleased﴾: the *lām* is the one that introduces the oath: that is, "and by Allah, he will surely be pleased with what We give him of honor and great reward." The majority recited *yarḍā* (يرضى) in the active voice, and it has also been recited in the passive.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿By the night when it covers﴾, that he said: "When it grows dark."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from Ibn Masʿud, who said: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq bought Bilal from Umayya ibn Khalaf and Ubayy ibn Khalaf in exchange for a striped cloak and ten ounces (of silver), and he freed him for the sake of Allah. So Allah revealed: "﴿By the night when it covers﴾" up to His saying: "﴿Indeed, your efforts are diverse﴾," (referring to) the efforts of Abu Bakr, Umayya, and Ubayy; up to His saying: "﴿and denied the best﴾," he said: "(That is) la ilaha illa Allah." Up to His saying: "﴿We will ease him toward difficulty﴾," he said: "The Fire."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: "﴿As for he who gives and fears (Allah)﴾," (the giving is) of wealth, "and fears (Allah)," he said: "fears his Lord." "﴿and believes in the best﴾," he said: "believes in the replacement from Allah." "﴿We will ease him toward ease﴾," he said: "toward the good from Allah." "﴿And as for he who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient﴾," he said: "He withholds his wealth and considers himself independent of his Lord." "﴿and denies the best﴾," he said: "(denies) the replacement from Allah." "﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾," he said: "toward evil from Allah."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him regarding "and believes in the best," he said: "He is certain of the replacement."

Ibn Jarir also narrated from him regarding "﴿and believes in the best﴾," he said: "He affirms la ilaha illa Allah." "﴿And as for he who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient﴾," he said: "He whom Allah has made wealthy, yet he withholds the zakat."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from ʿAmir ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: Abu Bakr used to free (slaves) for (embracing) Islam in Makkah, and he would free old women and women when they embraced Islam. His father said to him: "O my son, I see you freeing weak people. If only you would free strong men who would stand with you, protect you, and defend you." He said: "O father, I only desire what is with Allah." He said: "(p-1631) One of the people of my household told me that this verse was revealed concerning him: ﴿As for he who gives and fears, and believes in the best, We will ease him toward ease.﴾"

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: "﴿As for he who gives and fears, and believes in the best﴾," he said: (this refers to) Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. "﴿And as for he who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient, and denies the best﴾," he said: (this refers to) Abu Sufyan ibn Harb.

al-Bukhari, Muslim, the authors of the Sunan, and others narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) at a funeral, and he said: 'There is none among you but that his place in Paradise and his place in the Fire have been written.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall we not rely (on that)?' He said: 'Act, for each is made easy for what he was created for. As for the one who is among the people of happiness, he will be made easy for the deeds of the people of happiness; and as for the one who is among the people of wretchedness, he will be made easy for the deeds of the people of wretchedness.' Then he recited: ﴿As for he who gives and fears, and believes in the best﴾ up to His saying 'for hardship.'"

Ahmad, Muslim, and others narrated from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah that Suraqah ibn Malik said: "O Messenger of Allah, in what should we act? In a matter for which the decrees have been settled and the pens have run, or in a matter in which action is yet to be undertaken?" He said: "Rather, in a matter for which the decrees have been settled and the pens have run." Suraqah said: "Then why act, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Act, for each is made easy for what he was created for." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then recited this verse: ﴿As for he who gives and fears﴾ up to His saying ﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾ (32).

The hadith of ʿImran ibn Husayn has already been mentioned in the surah before this one, and there are hadiths on this matter through a group of the Companions.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "You will all surely enter Paradise except he who refuses." They said: "And who would refuse to enter Paradise?" Then he recited: ﴿He who denied and turned away﴾.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: "No one of this Ummah will remain but that Allah will admit him into Paradise, except one who runs away from Allah as a bad camel runs away from its owners. Whoever does not believe me, then Allah says: ﴿None will burn therein except the most wretched, who denied and turned away﴾," (meaning) he denied what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought and turned away from it.

Ahmad, al-Hakim, and al-Diya' narrated from Abu Umamah al-Bahili that he was asked about the gentlest word he had heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Surely all of you will be admitted by Allah into Paradise, except one who runs away from Allah as a camel runs away from its owners.'"

Ahmad, Ibn Majah, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "None enters the Fire except the wretched." It was said: "And who is the wretched?" He said: "The one who does not perform any obedience to Allah and does not abandon any disobedience to Allah."

Ahmad and al-Bukhari narrated from him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "All of my Ummah will enter Paradise on the Day of Resurrection except one who refuses." They said: "And who would refuse, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Whoever obeys me enters Paradise, and whoever disobeys me has refused."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿUrwah that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq freed seven, all of whom were tortured for the sake of Allah: Bilal, ʿAmir ibn Fuhayrah, al-Nahdiyyah and her daughter, Zinnirah, Umm ʿAys, and the slave woman of Banu al-Muammil. Concerning him was revealed: ﴿And the most righteous will be kept away from it﴾ up to the end of the surah.

al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from ʿAmir ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr what we mentioned earlier from him, with an addition: concerning him this verse was revealed: ﴿As for he who gives and fears, up to His saying: ﴿and no one has with him any favor to be repaid, except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High. And he will surely be satisfied.﴾

al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from him something similar through another chain.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And the most righteous will be kept away from it﴾, that he said: "He is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq."

This surah is Meccan according to the majority, though it has been said to be Madinan.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The surah of *By the night when it covers* was revealed in Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted the like of this from Ibn al-Zubayr.

al-Bayhaqi transmitted in his *Sunan* from Jabir ibn Samurah that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ and similar surahs in the Zuhr and 'Asr prayers."

al-Tabarani transmitted in *al-Awsat* from Anas that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led them in the midday prayer (al-hajirah), raised his voice, and recited ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ and ﴿By the night when it covers﴾. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, were you commanded in this prayer with something?' He said: 'No, but I wanted to set the time for you.'" The hadith "Why did you not pray with *Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High*, and *By the sun and its brightness*, and *By the night when it covers*" has already been mentioned.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "I say that this surah was revealed concerning generosity and miserliness: ﴿By the night when it covers﴾."

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.**

(p-1629) His saying ﴿By the night when it covers﴾: that is, it veils with its darkness what was luminous.

al-Zajjaj said: the night covers the horizon and everything between the heaven and the earth, so the light of the day departs. It was said that it covers the day, and it was said that it covers the earth. The first is preferable.

﴿And by the day when it displays itself﴾: that is, it appears, becomes clear and manifest, because the darkness that was in the night has been removed, and this happens with the rising of the sun.

﴿And by He who created the male and the female﴾: here *ma* (ما) is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*), meaning "and by He who (*alladhi*) created the male and the female." The word *ma* was used in place of *man* (من) to indicate the descriptive quality and for the purpose of glorification: that is, "and by the Mighty, Powerful One who created the two kinds, male and female."

al-Hasan and al-Kalbi said: its meaning is "and He who created the male and the female," so He would then have sworn by Himself.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: *wa ma khalaqa* (وما خلق) means *wa man khalaqa* (ومن خلق), "and He who created."

Muqatil said: the meaning is "and He created the male and the female," so *ma* (ما) in this view is a verbal-infinitive (*masdariyyah*).

al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: the meaning is Adam and Hawwa' (Eve). The apparent sense, however, is general.

The majority recited ﴿wa ma khalaqa al-dhakara wa al-untha﴾ (وما خلق الذكر والأنثى). Ibn Mas'ud recited *wa al-dhakari wa al-unthā* (والذكر والأنثى) without *ma khalaqa* (ما خلق).

﴿Indeed your efforts are diverse﴾: this is the answer to the oath. That is, indeed your deeds are different: among them is a deed for Paradise and among them is a deed for the Fire.

The majority of commentators said: *al-sa'y* (السعي) means work. So one strives to free his own soul, and another strives to ruin it. *Shatta* (شتى) is the plural of *shatit* (شتيت), like *marda* (مرضى) is the plural of *marid* (مريض). It was said that the diverse is called *shatta* because of the distance between its parts from one another.

﴿As for him who gives and fears (Allah)﴾: that is, he spends his wealth in the ways of good and guards against the prohibitions of Allah which He has forbidden.

﴿And affirms the best﴾: that is, with the replacement from Allah.

The commentators said: "As for him who gives" means he gives to those in hardship.

Qatadah said: he gives the right of Allah that is upon him.

al-Hasan said: he gives sincerity from his heart. "And affirms the best" means "there is no god but Allah." al-Dahhak and al-Sulami said likewise.

Mujahid said: "the best" means Paradise.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: "the best" means prayer, zakat and fasting. The first view is preferable.

Qatadah said: "the best" means the promise of Allah which He made to reward him.

al-Hasan said: "the best" means the replacement from His giving. Ibn Jarir chose this view.

﴿So We will ease him toward ease﴾: that is, We will prepare him for the good path, which is the doing of good. The meaning: We will make easy for him spending in the ways of good and acting in obedience to Allah.

al-Wahidi said: the commentators said that these verses were revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, who bought six of the believers who were in the hands of the people of Makkah and were being tortured by them for the sake of Allah.

﴿But as for him who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient﴾: that is, he withholds his wealth and does not spend it in the ways of good. "Considers himself self-sufficient" means he is indifferent to reward and recompense, or that he is self-sufficient through the desires of this world, away from the bliss of the Hereafter.

﴿And denies the best﴾: that is, the replacement from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Mujahid said: "the best" means the Garden. It was also narrated from him that he said: "there is no god but Allah."

﴿So We will ease him toward hardship﴾: that is, We will prepare him for the path of hardship and make it easy for him, until the means of good and righteousness become difficult for him and he becomes too weak to perform them, and that leads him to the Fire.

Muqatil said: it will be difficult for him to give anything good.

It was said: *al-'usra* (العسرى) means evil, because evil leads to punishment, and *al-'usra* is used of punishment. The meaning: We will prepare him for evil by causing it to come about through his own hands.

al-Farra' said: *sanuyassiruhu* (سنيسره) means *sanuhayyi'uhu* (سنهيئه), "We will prepare him." The Arabs say *qad yassarat al-ghanam* (قد يسرت الغنم) when the sheep give birth or make ready for giving birth.

The poet said:
They are two masters of ours who claim... and indeed they will rule over us if their sheep give birth.

﴿And his wealth will not avail him when he falls﴾: that is, the wealth he withheld will not avail him anything; or, "what will avail him when he falls," that is, when he perishes. It is said: *radiya al-rajulu yardā radan* (ردي الرجل يردى ردى), and *taradda yatarradda* (تردى يتردى), when he perished.

Qatadah, Abu Salih and Zayd ibn Aslam said: "when he falls" means when he falls into Hell. It is said *radiya fi al-bi'r* (ردي في البئر) and *taradda* (تردى) when he fell into it. It is also said: "I do not know where he went" (*ayna radiya*), that is, where did he go?

﴿Indeed, upon Us is the guidance﴾: this sentence is independent and confirms what precedes it. That is, upon Us is the clarification.

al-Zajjaj said: it is upon us to make clear the path of guidance from the path of misguidance.

Qatadah said: upon Allah is the clarification: the clarification of what He has made unlawful, and of obedience and disobedience.

al-Farra' said: whoever follows the path of guidance, upon Allah is his way, because of His saying ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way﴾ [16:9]. He means that whoever seeks Allah is on the straight path. al-Farra' also said: the meaning is "indeed upon Us is the guidance and the misguidance," and he omitted "misguidance," like His saying ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [16:81]. It was said that the meaning is: indeed upon Us is the reward of the guidance by which We guided him.

﴿And indeed, to Us belong the Hereafter and the first (life)﴾: that is, to Us belongs everything in the Hereafter, and everything in this world, which We dispose of as We will; whoever desires either of them or one of them should seek it from Us. It was said the meaning is: indeed, for Us is the reward of the Hereafter and the reward of this world.

﴿So I have warned you of a Fire that blazes﴾: that is, I have warned you and made you fear a fire that flames and blazes. Its original form is *tatalazzā* (تتلظى), and one of the two *tā'*s was omitted for lightness. Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Talhah ibn Musarrif recited it in the original form.

﴿None will burn therein except the most wretched﴾: that is, none will burn in it with a continuous, lasting burning except the most wretched, who is the disbeliever. If others among the disobedient burn in it, their burning is not like his. The phrase *yaslāhā* (يصلاها) means "enters it" or "experiences its heat."

Then He described the most wretched, saying: ﴿who denied and turned away﴾: that is, he denied the truth brought by the messengers and turned away from obedience and faith.

al-Farra' said: "*illa al-ashqā*" (إلا الأشقى) means except whoever was wretched in the knowledge of Allah, Majestic is His praise.

He also said: he did not deny by an outright rejection, but fell short of what he was commanded to do in obedience, so it was called denial, as you say: "Fulan met the enemy and denied (*fakhadhdhaba*)" when he drew back and retreated from following him.

al-Zajjaj said: this verse is the one on account of which the Murji'ah (*Murji'ah*, a sect that held that faith is not affected by deeds, and so that disobedience does not bring one into the Fire, the belief of those who hold *irja'*, postponement of judgment) argued for their position. They claimed that none enters the Fire except a disbeliever, and that the people of the Fire have degrees, among them that the hypocrites are at the lowest level of the Fire.

Allah, glory be to Him, whatever He promised with a particular kind of punishment, it is fitting that He punishes with it. He said: (p-1630) ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [4:48]. So if everyone who does not associate partners with Allah were not to be punished, then His saying "and forgives what is less than that for whom He wills" would have no benefit.

In *al-Kashshaf* it is said: the verse presents a comparison between two great states, that of the great polytheists and that of the great believers. So it intends to exaggerate the two contrasting attributes. "The most wretched" is mentioned and restricted to burning, as if the Fire was created only for him. "The most pious" is mentioned and restricted to salvation, as if Paradise was created only for him. It was said that "the most wretched" refers to Abu Jahl or Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and "the most pious" refers to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.

The meaning of ﴿and the most pious will be kept far from it﴾ (*wa sayujannabuha al-atqa*) is: the one who guards against disbelief with thorough guarding will be kept far away from it.

al-Wahidi said: "the most pious" is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq according to the consensus of all the commentators. End of quote. The preferable view is to take "the most wretched" and "the most pious" as applying to each one who has the two described attributes. The meaning then is: none will burn in it with a complete and continuous burning except the one who is perfect in wretchedness, who is the disbeliever. And none will be kept far from it, distanced completely, such that he does not even approach it, let alone enter it, except the one who is perfect in piety. This does not contradict the entry of some disobedient Muslims into the Fire in a non-continuous manner, nor the distancing from the Fire of some who are not perfect in piety, to a degree that does not reach the distancing of the one perfect in piety.

The conclusion is this: whoever among the Murji'ah holds to His saying ﴿None will burn therein except the most wretched﴾, claiming that "the most wretched" is the disbeliever because he is the one who denied and turned away, and that denial does not occur from disobedient Muslims, is told: what do you say about His saying ﴿and the most pious will be kept far from it﴾? It indicates that only the one perfect in piety is kept away from the Fire. So whoever is not perfect in piety, such as disobedient Muslims, is not among those kept away from the Fire. If you interpret "the most pious" in some way of interpretation, it binds you to the same for "the most wretched." So take these together, and be as the poet said:
I am content to bear love, and to come out of it neither against me nor for me.

It was said that by "the most wretched" and "the most pious" he meant "the wretched" and "the pious," as Tarafah ibn al-'Abd said:
Men wish that I would die, and if I die, that is a path in which I am not the only one.

Meaning: not the only one (*bi-wahid*). You are not unaware that this contradicts the description of "the most wretched" with denial, since that can only come from a disbeliever. So the purpose of the one who holds this view, that both attributes include disobedient Muslims, is not achieved.

Then He mentioned the attribute of "the most pious": ﴿who gives his wealth﴾, that is, he gives it and spends it in the ways of good. The phrase *yatazakkā* (يتزكى) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the subject of *yu'ti* (يؤتي), meaning: while he seeks to be pure before Allah, not seeking to show off or to be heard of. It may also be a substitute (*badal*) for *yu'ti*, being included with it within the relative clause.

The majority recited *yatazakkā*, the imperfect of *tazakkā*. 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Ali recited *yazzakkā* (يزكى), with the *tā'* assimilated into the *zāy*.

﴿And for no one has he a favor to be repaid﴾: this sentence is independent, confirming what precedes it, that the purification is sincere and free from anything that contradicts sincerity. That is, he is not one who gives his wealth in order to be repaid by someone's favor done to him, or to reward that person for it. Rather, he seeks by his charity the face of Allah, the Most High. The meaning is that there is no one among the people who has a favor upon him that deserves to be repaid, such that he intends by his giving to repay it. *Tujzā* (تجزى) was said in the imperfect passive for the sake of the rhyme of the verses; the original would be *yajziyuhā iyyāhu* (يجزيها إياه) or *yajziyuhu iyyāhā* (يجزيه إياها).

﴿Except seeking the face of his Lord, the Most High﴾: the majority recited *ibtighā'* (ابتغاء) in the accusative. It may be accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*, the object expressing the reason for the action), meaning: he gives only seeking the face of his Lord, the Most High. It may also be accusative as an object according to an interpretation, meaning: "I did not give you seeking your recompense, but seeking the face of Allah." Yahya ibn Wathhab recited it in the nominative, as a substitute (*badal*) for the position of *ni'mah* (نعمة), since its position is nominative either as subject or as the beginning of a sentence, and *min* (من) is extra. The nominative is the dialect of Tamim, for they permit substitution in the disconnected (exceptive) construction and treat it like the connected one.

Makki said: al-Farra' permitted the nominative of *ibtighā'* as a substitute for the position of *ni'mah*, but this is far-fetched.

Shihab al-Din said: it seems he (Makki) was unaware of it as a recitation. His regarding it as far-fetched is itself far-fetched, for it is a widespread dialect. The majority also recited *ibtighā'* with the long vowel, while Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited it with the short vowel (*qasr*).

*Al-A'lā* (الأعلى) is an adjective (*na't*) describing the Lord.

﴿And he will surely be pleased﴾: the *lām* is the one that introduces the oath: that is, "and by Allah, he will surely be pleased with what We give him of honor and great reward." The majority recited *yarḍā* (يرضى) in the active voice, and it has also been recited in the passive.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿By the night when it covers﴾, that he said: "When it grows dark."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from Ibn Masʿud, who said: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq bought Bilal from Umayya ibn Khalaf and Ubayy ibn Khalaf in exchange for a striped cloak and ten ounces (of silver), and he freed him for the sake of Allah. So Allah revealed: "﴿By the night when it covers﴾" up to His saying: "﴿Indeed, your efforts are diverse﴾," (referring to) the efforts of Abu Bakr, Umayya, and Ubayy; up to His saying: "﴿and denied the best﴾," he said: "(That is) la ilaha illa Allah." Up to His saying: "﴿We will ease him toward difficulty﴾," he said: "The Fire."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: "﴿As for he who gives and fears (Allah)﴾," (the giving is) of wealth, "and fears (Allah)," he said: "fears his Lord." "﴿and believes in the best﴾," he said: "believes in the replacement from Allah." "﴿We will ease him toward ease﴾," he said: "toward the good from Allah." "﴿And as for he who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient﴾," he said: "He withholds his wealth and considers himself independent of his Lord." "﴿and denies the best﴾," he said: "(denies) the replacement from Allah." "﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾," he said: "toward evil from Allah."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him regarding "and believes in the best," he said: "He is certain of the replacement."

Ibn Jarir also narrated from him regarding "﴿and believes in the best﴾," he said: "He affirms la ilaha illa Allah." "﴿And as for he who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient﴾," he said: "He whom Allah has made wealthy, yet he withholds the zakat."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from ʿAmir ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: Abu Bakr used to free (slaves) for (embracing) Islam in Makkah, and he would free old women and women when they embraced Islam. His father said to him: "O my son, I see you freeing weak people. If only you would free strong men who would stand with you, protect you, and defend you." He said: "O father, I only desire what is with Allah." He said: "(p-1631) One of the people of my household told me that this verse was revealed concerning him: ﴿As for he who gives and fears, and believes in the best, We will ease him toward ease.﴾"

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: "﴿As for he who gives and fears, and believes in the best﴾," he said: (this refers to) Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. "﴿And as for he who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient, and denies the best﴾," he said: (this refers to) Abu Sufyan ibn Harb.

al-Bukhari, Muslim, the authors of the Sunan, and others narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) at a funeral, and he said: 'There is none among you but that his place in Paradise and his place in the Fire have been written.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall we not rely (on that)?' He said: 'Act, for each is made easy for what he was created for. As for the one who is among the people of happiness, he will be made easy for the deeds of the people of happiness; and as for the one who is among the people of wretchedness, he will be made easy for the deeds of the people of wretchedness.' Then he recited: ﴿As for he who gives and fears, and believes in the best﴾ up to His saying 'for hardship.'"

Ahmad, Muslim, and others narrated from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah that Suraqah ibn Malik said: "O Messenger of Allah, in what should we act? In a matter for which the decrees have been settled and the pens have run, or in a matter in which action is yet to be undertaken?" He said: "Rather, in a matter for which the decrees have been settled and the pens have run." Suraqah said: "Then why act, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Act, for each is made easy for what he was created for." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then recited this verse: ﴿As for he who gives and fears﴾ up to His saying ﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾ (32).

The hadith of ʿImran ibn Husayn has already been mentioned in the surah before this one, and there are hadiths on this matter through a group of the Companions.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "You will all surely enter Paradise except he who refuses." They said: "And who would refuse to enter Paradise?" Then he recited: ﴿He who denied and turned away﴾.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: "No one of this Ummah will remain but that Allah will admit him into Paradise, except one who runs away from Allah as a bad camel runs away from its owners. Whoever does not believe me, then Allah says: ﴿None will burn therein except the most wretched, who denied and turned away﴾," (meaning) he denied what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought and turned away from it.

Ahmad, al-Hakim, and al-Diya' narrated from Abu Umamah al-Bahili that he was asked about the gentlest word he had heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Surely all of you will be admitted by Allah into Paradise, except one who runs away from Allah as a camel runs away from its owners.'"

Ahmad, Ibn Majah, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "None enters the Fire except the wretched." It was said: "And who is the wretched?" He said: "The one who does not perform any obedience to Allah and does not abandon any disobedience to Allah."

Ahmad and al-Bukhari narrated from him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "All of my Ummah will enter Paradise on the Day of Resurrection except one who refuses." They said: "And who would refuse, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Whoever obeys me enters Paradise, and whoever disobeys me has refused."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿUrwah that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq freed seven, all of whom were tortured for the sake of Allah: Bilal, ʿAmir ibn Fuhayrah, al-Nahdiyyah and her daughter, Zinnirah, Umm ʿAys, and the slave woman of Banu al-Muammil. Concerning him was revealed: ﴿And the most righteous will be kept away from it﴾ up to the end of the surah.

al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from ʿAmir ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr what we mentioned earlier from him, with an addition: concerning him this verse was revealed: ﴿As for he who gives and fears, up to His saying: ﴿and no one has with him any favor to be repaid, except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High. And he will surely be satisfied.﴾

al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from him something similar through another chain.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And the most righteous will be kept away from it﴾, that he said: "He is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq."

This surah is Meccan according to the majority, though it has been said to be Madinan.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The surah of *By the night when it covers* was revealed in Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted the like of this from Ibn al-Zubayr.

al-Bayhaqi transmitted in his *Sunan* from Jabir ibn Samurah that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ and similar surahs in the Zuhr and 'Asr prayers."

al-Tabarani transmitted in *al-Awsat* from Anas that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led them in the midday prayer (al-hajirah), raised his voice, and recited ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ and ﴿By the night when it covers﴾. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, were you commanded in this prayer with something?' He said: 'No, but I wanted to set the time for you.'" The hadith "Why did you not pray with *Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High*, and *By the sun and its brightness*, and *By the night when it covers*" has already been mentioned.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "I say that this surah was revealed concerning generosity and miserliness: ﴿By the night when it covers﴾."

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.**

(p-1629) His saying ﴿By the night when it covers﴾: that is, it veils with its darkness what was luminous.

al-Zajjaj said: the night covers the horizon and everything between the heaven and the earth, so the light of the day departs. It was said that it covers the day, and it was said that it covers the earth. The first is preferable.

﴿And by the day when it displays itself﴾: that is, it appears, becomes clear and manifest, because the darkness that was in the night has been removed, and this happens with the rising of the sun.

﴿And by He who created the male and the female﴾: here *ma* (ما) is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*), meaning "and by He who (*alladhi*) created the male and the female." The word *ma* was used in place of *man* (من) to indicate the descriptive quality and for the purpose of glorification: that is, "and by the Mighty, Powerful One who created the two kinds, male and female."

al-Hasan and al-Kalbi said: its meaning is "and He who created the male and the female," so He would then have sworn by Himself.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: *wa ma khalaqa* (وما خلق) means *wa man khalaqa* (ومن خلق), "and He who created."

Muqatil said: the meaning is "and He created the male and the female," so *ma* (ما) in this view is a verbal-infinitive (*masdariyyah*).

al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: the meaning is Adam and Hawwa' (Eve). The apparent sense, however, is general.

The majority recited ﴿wa ma khalaqa al-dhakara wa al-untha﴾ (وما خلق الذكر والأنثى). Ibn Mas'ud recited *wa al-dhakari wa al-unthā* (والذكر والأنثى) without *ma khalaqa* (ما خلق).

﴿Indeed your efforts are diverse﴾: this is the answer to the oath. That is, indeed your deeds are different: among them is a deed for Paradise and among them is a deed for the Fire.

The majority of commentators said: *al-sa'y* (السعي) means work. So one strives to free his own soul, and another strives to ruin it. *Shatta* (شتى) is the plural of *shatit* (شتيت), like *marda* (مرضى) is the plural of *marid* (مريض). It was said that the diverse is called *shatta* because of the distance between its parts from one another.

﴿As for him who gives and fears (Allah)﴾: that is, he spends his wealth in the ways of good and guards against the prohibitions of Allah which He has forbidden.

﴿And affirms the best﴾: that is, with the replacement from Allah.

The commentators said: "As for him who gives" means he gives to those in hardship.

Qatadah said: he gives the right of Allah that is upon him.

al-Hasan said: he gives sincerity from his heart. "And affirms the best" means "there is no god but Allah." al-Dahhak and al-Sulami said likewise.

Mujahid said: "the best" means Paradise.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: "the best" means prayer, zakat and fasting. The first view is preferable.

Qatadah said: "the best" means the promise of Allah which He made to reward him.

al-Hasan said: "the best" means the replacement from His giving. Ibn Jarir chose this view.

﴿So We will ease him toward ease﴾: that is, We will prepare him for the good path, which is the doing of good. The meaning: We will make easy for him spending in the ways of good and acting in obedience to Allah.

al-Wahidi said: the commentators said that these verses were revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, who bought six of the believers who were in the hands of the people of Makkah and were being tortured by them for the sake of Allah.

﴿But as for him who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient﴾: that is, he withholds his wealth and does not spend it in the ways of good. "Considers himself self-sufficient" means he is indifferent to reward and recompense, or that he is self-sufficient through the desires of this world, away from the bliss of the Hereafter.

﴿And denies the best﴾: that is, the replacement from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Mujahid said: "the best" means the Garden. It was also narrated from him that he said: "there is no god but Allah."

﴿So We will ease him toward hardship﴾: that is, We will prepare him for the path of hardship and make it easy for him, until the means of good and righteousness become difficult for him and he becomes too weak to perform them, and that leads him to the Fire.

Muqatil said: it will be difficult for him to give anything good.

It was said: *al-'usra* (العسرى) means evil, because evil leads to punishment, and *al-'usra* is used of punishment. The meaning: We will prepare him for evil by causing it to come about through his own hands.

al-Farra' said: *sanuyassiruhu* (سنيسره) means *sanuhayyi'uhu* (سنهيئه), "We will prepare him." The Arabs say *qad yassarat al-ghanam* (قد يسرت الغنم) when the sheep give birth or make ready for giving birth.

The poet said:
They are two masters of ours who claim... and indeed they will rule over us if their sheep give birth.

﴿And his wealth will not avail him when he falls﴾: that is, the wealth he withheld will not avail him anything; or, "what will avail him when he falls," that is, when he perishes. It is said: *radiya al-rajulu yardā radan* (ردي الرجل يردى ردى), and *taradda yatarradda* (تردى يتردى), when he perished.

Qatadah, Abu Salih and Zayd ibn Aslam said: "when he falls" means when he falls into Hell. It is said *radiya fi al-bi'r* (ردي في البئر) and *taradda* (تردى) when he fell into it. It is also said: "I do not know where he went" (*ayna radiya*), that is, where did he go?

﴿Indeed, upon Us is the guidance﴾: this sentence is independent and confirms what precedes it. That is, upon Us is the clarification.

al-Zajjaj said: it is upon us to make clear the path of guidance from the path of misguidance.

Qatadah said: upon Allah is the clarification: the clarification of what He has made unlawful, and of obedience and disobedience.

al-Farra' said: whoever follows the path of guidance, upon Allah is his way, because of His saying ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way﴾ [16:9]. He means that whoever seeks Allah is on the straight path. al-Farra' also said: the meaning is "indeed upon Us is the guidance and the misguidance," and he omitted "misguidance," like His saying ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [16:81]. It was said that the meaning is: indeed upon Us is the reward of the guidance by which We guided him.

﴿And indeed, to Us belong the Hereafter and the first (life)﴾: that is, to Us belongs everything in the Hereafter, and everything in this world, which We dispose of as We will; whoever desires either of them or one of them should seek it from Us. It was said the meaning is: indeed, for Us is the reward of the Hereafter and the reward of this world.

﴿So I have warned you of a Fire that blazes﴾: that is, I have warned you and made you fear a fire that flames and blazes. Its original form is *tatalazzā* (تتلظى), and one of the two *tā'*s was omitted for lightness. Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Talhah ibn Musarrif recited it in the original form.

﴿None will burn therein except the most wretched﴾: that is, none will burn in it with a continuous, lasting burning except the most wretched, who is the disbeliever. If others among the disobedient burn in it, their burning is not like his. The phrase *yaslāhā* (يصلاها) means "enters it" or "experiences its heat."

Then He described the most wretched, saying: ﴿who denied and turned away﴾: that is, he denied the truth brought by the messengers and turned away from obedience and faith.

al-Farra' said: "*illa al-ashqā*" (إلا الأشقى) means except whoever was wretched in the knowledge of Allah, Majestic is His praise.

He also said: he did not deny by an outright rejection, but fell short of what he was commanded to do in obedience, so it was called denial, as you say: "Fulan met the enemy and denied (*fakhadhdhaba*)" when he drew back and retreated from following him.

al-Zajjaj said: this verse is the one on account of which the Murji'ah (*Murji'ah*, a sect that held that faith is not affected by deeds, and so that disobedience does not bring one into the Fire, the belief of those who hold *irja'*, postponement of judgment) argued for their position. They claimed that none enters the Fire except a disbeliever, and that the people of the Fire have degrees, among them that the hypocrites are at the lowest level of the Fire.

Allah, glory be to Him, whatever He promised with a particular kind of punishment, it is fitting that He punishes with it. He said: (p-1630) ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [4:48]. So if everyone who does not associate partners with Allah were not to be punished, then His saying "and forgives what is less than that for whom He wills" would have no benefit.

In *al-Kashshaf* it is said: the verse presents a comparison between two great states, that of the great polytheists and that of the great believers. So it intends to exaggerate the two contrasting attributes. "The most wretched" is mentioned and restricted to burning, as if the Fire was created only for him. "The most pious" is mentioned and restricted to salvation, as if Paradise was created only for him. It was said that "the most wretched" refers to Abu Jahl or Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and "the most pious" refers to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.

The meaning of ﴿and the most pious will be kept far from it﴾ (*wa sayujannabuha al-atqa*) is: the one who guards against disbelief with thorough guarding will be kept far away from it.

al-Wahidi said: "the most pious" is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq according to the consensus of all the commentators. End of quote. The preferable view is to take "the most wretched" and "the most pious" as applying to each one who has the two described attributes. The meaning then is: none will burn in it with a complete and continuous burning except the one who is perfect in wretchedness, who is the disbeliever. And none will be kept far from it, distanced completely, such that he does not even approach it, let alone enter it, except the one who is perfect in piety. This does not contradict the entry of some disobedient Muslims into the Fire in a non-continuous manner, nor the distancing from the Fire of some who are not perfect in piety, to a degree that does not reach the distancing of the one perfect in piety.

The conclusion is this: whoever among the Murji'ah holds to His saying ﴿None will burn therein except the most wretched﴾, claiming that "the most wretched" is the disbeliever because he is the one who denied and turned away, and that denial does not occur from disobedient Muslims, is told: what do you say about His saying ﴿and the most pious will be kept far from it﴾? It indicates that only the one perfect in piety is kept away from the Fire. So whoever is not perfect in piety, such as disobedient Muslims, is not among those kept away from the Fire. If you interpret "the most pious" in some way of interpretation, it binds you to the same for "the most wretched." So take these together, and be as the poet said:
I am content to bear love, and to come out of it neither against me nor for me.

It was said that by "the most wretched" and "the most pious" he meant "the wretched" and "the pious," as Tarafah ibn al-'Abd said:
Men wish that I would die, and if I die, that is a path in which I am not the only one.

Meaning: not the only one (*bi-wahid*). You are not unaware that this contradicts the description of "the most wretched" with denial, since that can only come from a disbeliever. So the purpose of the one who holds this view, that both attributes include disobedient Muslims, is not achieved.

Then He mentioned the attribute of "the most pious": ﴿who gives his wealth﴾, that is, he gives it and spends it in the ways of good. The phrase *yatazakkā* (يتزكى) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the subject of *yu'ti* (يؤتي), meaning: while he seeks to be pure before Allah, not seeking to show off or to be heard of. It may also be a substitute (*badal*) for *yu'ti*, being included with it within the relative clause.

The majority recited *yatazakkā*, the imperfect of *tazakkā*. 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Ali recited *yazzakkā* (يزكى), with the *tā'* assimilated into the *zāy*.

﴿And for no one has he a favor to be repaid﴾: this sentence is independent, confirming what precedes it, that the purification is sincere and free from anything that contradicts sincerity. That is, he is not one who gives his wealth in order to be repaid by someone's favor done to him, or to reward that person for it. Rather, he seeks by his charity the face of Allah, the Most High. The meaning is that there is no one among the people who has a favor upon him that deserves to be repaid, such that he intends by his giving to repay it. *Tujzā* (تجزى) was said in the imperfect passive for the sake of the rhyme of the verses; the original would be *yajziyuhā iyyāhu* (يجزيها إياه) or *yajziyuhu iyyāhā* (يجزيه إياها).

﴿Except seeking the face of his Lord, the Most High﴾: the majority recited *ibtighā'* (ابتغاء) in the accusative. It may be accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*, the object expressing the reason for the action), meaning: he gives only seeking the face of his Lord, the Most High. It may also be accusative as an object according to an interpretation, meaning: "I did not give you seeking your recompense, but seeking the face of Allah." Yahya ibn Wathhab recited it in the nominative, as a substitute (*badal*) for the position of *ni'mah* (نعمة), since its position is nominative either as subject or as the beginning of a sentence, and *min* (من) is extra. The nominative is the dialect of Tamim, for they permit substitution in the disconnected (exceptive) construction and treat it like the connected one.

Makki said: al-Farra' permitted the nominative of *ibtighā'* as a substitute for the position of *ni'mah*, but this is far-fetched.

Shihab al-Din said: it seems he (Makki) was unaware of it as a recitation. His regarding it as far-fetched is itself far-fetched, for it is a widespread dialect. The majority also recited *ibtighā'* with the long vowel, while Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited it with the short vowel (*qasr*).

*Al-A'lā* (الأعلى) is an adjective (*na't*) describing the Lord.

﴿And he will surely be pleased﴾: the *lām* is the one that introduces the oath: that is, "and by Allah, he will surely be pleased with what We give him of honor and great reward." The majority recited *yarḍā* (يرضى) in the active voice, and it has also been recited in the passive.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿By the night when it covers﴾, that he said: "When it grows dark."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from Ibn Masʿud, who said: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq bought Bilal from Umayya ibn Khalaf and Ubayy ibn Khalaf in exchange for a striped cloak and ten ounces (of silver), and he freed him for the sake of Allah. So Allah revealed: "﴿By the night when it covers﴾" up to His saying: "﴿Indeed, your efforts are diverse﴾," (referring to) the efforts of Abu Bakr, Umayya, and Ubayy; up to His saying: "﴿and denied the best﴾," he said: "(That is) la ilaha illa Allah." Up to His saying: "﴿We will ease him toward difficulty﴾," he said: "The Fire."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: "﴿As for he who gives and fears (Allah)﴾," (the giving is) of wealth, "and fears (Allah)," he said: "fears his Lord." "﴿and believes in the best﴾," he said: "believes in the replacement from Allah." "﴿We will ease him toward ease﴾," he said: "toward the good from Allah." "﴿And as for he who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient﴾," he said: "He withholds his wealth and considers himself independent of his Lord." "﴿and denies the best﴾," he said: "(denies) the replacement from Allah." "﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾," he said: "toward evil from Allah."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him regarding "and believes in the best," he said: "He is certain of the replacement."

Ibn Jarir also narrated from him regarding "﴿and believes in the best﴾," he said: "He affirms la ilaha illa Allah." "﴿And as for he who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient﴾," he said: "He whom Allah has made wealthy, yet he withholds the zakat."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from ʿAmir ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: Abu Bakr used to free (slaves) for (embracing) Islam in Makkah, and he would free old women and women when they embraced Islam. His father said to him: "O my son, I see you freeing weak people. If only you would free strong men who would stand with you, protect you, and defend you." He said: "O father, I only desire what is with Allah." He said: "(p-1631) One of the people of my household told me that this verse was revealed concerning him: ﴿As for he who gives and fears, and believes in the best, We will ease him toward ease.﴾"

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: "﴿As for he who gives and fears, and believes in the best﴾," he said: (this refers to) Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. "﴿And as for he who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient, and denies the best﴾," he said: (this refers to) Abu Sufyan ibn Harb.

al-Bukhari, Muslim, the authors of the Sunan, and others narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) at a funeral, and he said: 'There is none among you but that his place in Paradise and his place in the Fire have been written.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall we not rely (on that)?' He said: 'Act, for each is made easy for what he was created for. As for the one who is among the people of happiness, he will be made easy for the deeds of the people of happiness; and as for the one who is among the people of wretchedness, he will be made easy for the deeds of the people of wretchedness.' Then he recited: ﴿As for he who gives and fears, and believes in the best﴾ up to His saying 'for hardship.'"

Ahmad, Muslim, and others narrated from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah that Suraqah ibn Malik said: "O Messenger of Allah, in what should we act? In a matter for which the decrees have been settled and the pens have run, or in a matter in which action is yet to be undertaken?" He said: "Rather, in a matter for which the decrees have been settled and the pens have run." Suraqah said: "Then why act, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Act, for each is made easy for what he was created for." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then recited this verse: ﴿As for he who gives and fears﴾ up to His saying ﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾ (32).

The hadith of ʿImran ibn Husayn has already been mentioned in the surah before this one, and there are hadiths on this matter through a group of the Companions.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "You will all surely enter Paradise except he who refuses." They said: "And who would refuse to enter Paradise?" Then he recited: ﴿He who denied and turned away﴾.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: "No one of this Ummah will remain but that Allah will admit him into Paradise, except one who runs away from Allah as a bad camel runs away from its owners. Whoever does not believe me, then Allah says: ﴿None will burn therein except the most wretched, who denied and turned away﴾," (meaning) he denied what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought and turned away from it.

Ahmad, al-Hakim, and al-Diya' narrated from Abu Umamah al-Bahili that he was asked about the gentlest word he had heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Surely all of you will be admitted by Allah into Paradise, except one who runs away from Allah as a camel runs away from its owners.'"

Ahmad, Ibn Majah, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "None enters the Fire except the wretched." It was said: "And who is the wretched?" He said: "The one who does not perform any obedience to Allah and does not abandon any disobedience to Allah."

Ahmad and al-Bukhari narrated from him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "All of my Ummah will enter Paradise on the Day of Resurrection except one who refuses." They said: "And who would refuse, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Whoever obeys me enters Paradise, and whoever disobeys me has refused."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿUrwah that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq freed seven, all of whom were tortured for the sake of Allah: Bilal, ʿAmir ibn Fuhayrah, al-Nahdiyyah and her daughter, Zinnirah, Umm ʿAys, and the slave woman of Banu al-Muammil. Concerning him was revealed: ﴿And the most righteous will be kept away from it﴾ up to the end of the surah.

al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from ʿAmir ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr what we mentioned earlier from him, with an addition: concerning him this verse was revealed: ﴿As for he who gives and fears, up to His saying: ﴿and no one has with him any favor to be repaid, except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High. And he will surely be satisfied.﴾

al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from him something similar through another chain.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And the most righteous will be kept away from it﴾, that he said: "He is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq."

This surah is Meccan according to the majority, though it has been said to be Madinan.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The surah of *By the night when it covers* was revealed in Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted the like of this from Ibn al-Zubayr.

al-Bayhaqi transmitted in his *Sunan* from Jabir ibn Samurah that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ and similar surahs in the Zuhr and 'Asr prayers."

al-Tabarani transmitted in *al-Awsat* from Anas that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led them in the midday prayer (al-hajirah), raised his voice, and recited ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ and ﴿By the night when it covers﴾. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, were you commanded in this prayer with something?' He said: 'No, but I wanted to set the time for you.'" The hadith "Why did you not pray with *Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High*, and *By the sun and its brightness*, and *By the night when it covers*" has already been mentioned.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "I say that this surah was revealed concerning generosity and miserliness: ﴿By the night when it covers﴾."

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.**

(p-1629) His saying ﴿By the night when it covers﴾: that is, it veils with its darkness what was luminous.

al-Zajjaj said: the night covers the horizon and everything between the heaven and the earth, so the light of the day departs. It was said that it covers the day, and it was said that it covers the earth. The first is preferable.

﴿And by the day when it displays itself﴾: that is, it appears, becomes clear and manifest, because the darkness that was in the night has been removed, and this happens with the rising of the sun.

﴿And by He who created the male and the female﴾: here *ma* (ما) is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*), meaning "and by He who (*alladhi*) created the male and the female." The word *ma* was used in place of *man* (من) to indicate the descriptive quality and for the purpose of glorification: that is, "and by the Mighty, Powerful One who created the two kinds, male and female."

al-Hasan and al-Kalbi said: its meaning is "and He who created the male and the female," so He would then have sworn by Himself.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: *wa ma khalaqa* (وما خلق) means *wa man khalaqa* (ومن خلق), "and He who created."

Muqatil said: the meaning is "and He created the male and the female," so *ma* (ما) in this view is a verbal-infinitive (*masdariyyah*).

al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: the meaning is Adam and Hawwa' (Eve). The apparent sense, however, is general.

The majority recited ﴿wa ma khalaqa al-dhakara wa al-untha﴾ (وما خلق الذكر والأنثى). Ibn Mas'ud recited *wa al-dhakari wa al-unthā* (والذكر والأنثى) without *ma khalaqa* (ما خلق).

﴿Indeed your efforts are diverse﴾: this is the answer to the oath. That is, indeed your deeds are different: among them is a deed for Paradise and among them is a deed for the Fire.

The majority of commentators said: *al-sa'y* (السعي) means work. So one strives to free his own soul, and another strives to ruin it. *Shatta* (شتى) is the plural of *shatit* (شتيت), like *marda* (مرضى) is the plural of *marid* (مريض). It was said that the diverse is called *shatta* because of the distance between its parts from one another.

﴿As for him who gives and fears (Allah)﴾: that is, he spends his wealth in the ways of good and guards against the prohibitions of Allah which He has forbidden.

﴿And affirms the best﴾: that is, with the replacement from Allah.

The commentators said: "As for him who gives" means he gives to those in hardship.

Qatadah said: he gives the right of Allah that is upon him.

al-Hasan said: he gives sincerity from his heart. "And affirms the best" means "there is no god but Allah." al-Dahhak and al-Sulami said likewise.

Mujahid said: "the best" means Paradise.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: "the best" means prayer, zakat and fasting. The first view is preferable.

Qatadah said: "the best" means the promise of Allah which He made to reward him.

al-Hasan said: "the best" means the replacement from His giving. Ibn Jarir chose this view.

﴿So We will ease him toward ease﴾: that is, We will prepare him for the good path, which is the doing of good. The meaning: We will make easy for him spending in the ways of good and acting in obedience to Allah.

al-Wahidi said: the commentators said that these verses were revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, who bought six of the believers who were in the hands of the people of Makkah and were being tortured by them for the sake of Allah.

﴿But as for him who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient﴾: that is, he withholds his wealth and does not spend it in the ways of good. "Considers himself self-sufficient" means he is indifferent to reward and recompense, or that he is self-sufficient through the desires of this world, away from the bliss of the Hereafter.

﴿And denies the best﴾: that is, the replacement from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Mujahid said: "the best" means the Garden. It was also narrated from him that he said: "there is no god but Allah."

﴿So We will ease him toward hardship﴾: that is, We will prepare him for the path of hardship and make it easy for him, until the means of good and righteousness become difficult for him and he becomes too weak to perform them, and that leads him to the Fire.

Muqatil said: it will be difficult for him to give anything good.

It was said: *al-'usra* (العسرى) means evil, because evil leads to punishment, and *al-'usra* is used of punishment. The meaning: We will prepare him for evil by causing it to come about through his own hands.

al-Farra' said: *sanuyassiruhu* (سنيسره) means *sanuhayyi'uhu* (سنهيئه), "We will prepare him." The Arabs say *qad yassarat al-ghanam* (قد يسرت الغنم) when the sheep give birth or make ready for giving birth.

The poet said:
They are two masters of ours who claim... and indeed they will rule over us if their sheep give birth.

﴿And his wealth will not avail him when he falls﴾: that is, the wealth he withheld will not avail him anything; or, "what will avail him when he falls," that is, when he perishes. It is said: *radiya al-rajulu yardā radan* (ردي الرجل يردى ردى), and *taradda yatarradda* (تردى يتردى), when he perished.

Qatadah, Abu Salih and Zayd ibn Aslam said: "when he falls" means when he falls into Hell. It is said *radiya fi al-bi'r* (ردي في البئر) and *taradda* (تردى) when he fell into it. It is also said: "I do not know where he went" (*ayna radiya*), that is, where did he go?

﴿Indeed, upon Us is the guidance﴾: this sentence is independent and confirms what precedes it. That is, upon Us is the clarification.

al-Zajjaj said: it is upon us to make clear the path of guidance from the path of misguidance.

Qatadah said: upon Allah is the clarification: the clarification of what He has made unlawful, and of obedience and disobedience.

al-Farra' said: whoever follows the path of guidance, upon Allah is his way, because of His saying ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way﴾ [16:9]. He means that whoever seeks Allah is on the straight path. al-Farra' also said: the meaning is "indeed upon Us is the guidance and the misguidance," and he omitted "misguidance," like His saying ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [16:81]. It was said that the meaning is: indeed upon Us is the reward of the guidance by which We guided him.

﴿And indeed, to Us belong the Hereafter and the first (life)﴾: that is, to Us belongs everything in the Hereafter, and everything in this world, which We dispose of as We will; whoever desires either of them or one of them should seek it from Us. It was said the meaning is: indeed, for Us is the reward of the Hereafter and the reward of this world.

﴿So I have warned you of a Fire that blazes﴾: that is, I have warned you and made you fear a fire that flames and blazes. Its original form is *tatalazzā* (تتلظى), and one of the two *tā'*s was omitted for lightness. Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Talhah ibn Musarrif recited it in the original form.

﴿None will burn therein except the most wretched﴾: that is, none will burn in it with a continuous, lasting burning except the most wretched, who is the disbeliever. If others among the disobedient burn in it, their burning is not like his. The phrase *yaslāhā* (يصلاها) means "enters it" or "experiences its heat."

Then He described the most wretched, saying: ﴿who denied and turned away﴾: that is, he denied the truth brought by the messengers and turned away from obedience and faith.

al-Farra' said: "*illa al-ashqā*" (إلا الأشقى) means except whoever was wretched in the knowledge of Allah, Majestic is His praise.

He also said: he did not deny by an outright rejection, but fell short of what he was commanded to do in obedience, so it was called denial, as you say: "Fulan met the enemy and denied (*fakhadhdhaba*)" when he drew back and retreated from following him.

al-Zajjaj said: this verse is the one on account of which the Murji'ah (*Murji'ah*, a sect that held that faith is not affected by deeds, and so that disobedience does not bring one into the Fire, the belief of those who hold *irja'*, postponement of judgment) argued for their position. They claimed that none enters the Fire except a disbeliever, and that the people of the Fire have degrees, among them that the hypocrites are at the lowest level of the Fire.

Allah, glory be to Him, whatever He promised with a particular kind of punishment, it is fitting that He punishes with it. He said: (p-1630) ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [4:48]. So if everyone who does not associate partners with Allah were not to be punished, then His saying "and forgives what is less than that for whom He wills" would have no benefit.

In *al-Kashshaf* it is said: the verse presents a comparison between two great states, that of the great polytheists and that of the great believers. So it intends to exaggerate the two contrasting attributes. "The most wretched" is mentioned and restricted to burning, as if the Fire was created only for him. "The most pious" is mentioned and restricted to salvation, as if Paradise was created only for him. It was said that "the most wretched" refers to Abu Jahl or Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and "the most pious" refers to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.

The meaning of ﴿and the most pious will be kept far from it﴾ (*wa sayujannabuha al-atqa*) is: the one who guards against disbelief with thorough guarding will be kept far away from it.

al-Wahidi said: "the most pious" is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq according to the consensus of all the commentators. End of quote. The preferable view is to take "the most wretched" and "the most pious" as applying to each one who has the two described attributes. The meaning then is: none will burn in it with a complete and continuous burning except the one who is perfect in wretchedness, who is the disbeliever. And none will be kept far from it, distanced completely, such that he does not even approach it, let alone enter it, except the one who is perfect in piety. This does not contradict the entry of some disobedient Muslims into the Fire in a non-continuous manner, nor the distancing from the Fire of some who are not perfect in piety, to a degree that does not reach the distancing of the one perfect in piety.

The conclusion is this: whoever among the Murji'ah holds to His saying ﴿None will burn therein except the most wretched﴾, claiming that "the most wretched" is the disbeliever because he is the one who denied and turned away, and that denial does not occur from disobedient Muslims, is told: what do you say about His saying ﴿and the most pious will be kept far from it﴾? It indicates that only the one perfect in piety is kept away from the Fire. So whoever is not perfect in piety, such as disobedient Muslims, is not among those kept away from the Fire. If you interpret "the most pious" in some way of interpretation, it binds you to the same for "the most wretched." So take these together, and be as the poet said:
I am content to bear love, and to come out of it neither against me nor for me.

It was said that by "the most wretched" and "the most pious" he meant "the wretched" and "the pious," as Tarafah ibn al-'Abd said:
Men wish that I would die, and if I die, that is a path in which I am not the only one.

Meaning: not the only one (*bi-wahid*). You are not unaware that this contradicts the description of "the most wretched" with denial, since that can only come from a disbeliever. So the purpose of the one who holds this view, that both attributes include disobedient Muslims, is not achieved.

Then He mentioned the attribute of "the most pious": ﴿who gives his wealth﴾, that is, he gives it and spends it in the ways of good. The phrase *yatazakkā* (يتزكى) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the subject of *yu'ti* (يؤتي), meaning: while he seeks to be pure before Allah, not seeking to show off or to be heard of. It may also be a substitute (*badal*) for *yu'ti*, being included with it within the relative clause.

The majority recited *yatazakkā*, the imperfect of *tazakkā*. 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Ali recited *yazzakkā* (يزكى), with the *tā'* assimilated into the *zāy*.

﴿And for no one has he a favor to be repaid﴾: this sentence is independent, confirming what precedes it, that the purification is sincere and free from anything that contradicts sincerity. That is, he is not one who gives his wealth in order to be repaid by someone's favor done to him, or to reward that person for it. Rather, he seeks by his charity the face of Allah, the Most High. The meaning is that there is no one among the people who has a favor upon him that deserves to be repaid, such that he intends by his giving to repay it. *Tujzā* (تجزى) was said in the imperfect passive for the sake of the rhyme of the verses; the original would be *yajziyuhā iyyāhu* (يجزيها إياه) or *yajziyuhu iyyāhā* (يجزيه إياها).

﴿Except seeking the face of his Lord, the Most High﴾: the majority recited *ibtighā'* (ابتغاء) in the accusative. It may be accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*, the object expressing the reason for the action), meaning: he gives only seeking the face of his Lord, the Most High. It may also be accusative as an object according to an interpretation, meaning: "I did not give you seeking your recompense, but seeking the face of Allah." Yahya ibn Wathhab recited it in the nominative, as a substitute (*badal*) for the position of *ni'mah* (نعمة), since its position is nominative either as subject or as the beginning of a sentence, and *min* (من) is extra. The nominative is the dialect of Tamim, for they permit substitution in the disconnected (exceptive) construction and treat it like the connected one.

Makki said: al-Farra' permitted the nominative of *ibtighā'* as a substitute for the position of *ni'mah*, but this is far-fetched.

Shihab al-Din said: it seems he (Makki) was unaware of it as a recitation. His regarding it as far-fetched is itself far-fetched, for it is a widespread dialect. The majority also recited *ibtighā'* with the long vowel, while Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited it with the short vowel (*qasr*).

*Al-A'lā* (الأعلى) is an adjective (*na't*) describing the Lord.

﴿And he will surely be pleased﴾: the *lām* is the one that introduces the oath: that is, "and by Allah, he will surely be pleased with what We give him of honor and great reward." The majority recited *yarḍā* (يرضى) in the active voice, and it has also been recited in the passive.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿By the night when it covers﴾, that he said: "When it grows dark."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from Ibn Masʿud, who said: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq bought Bilal from Umayya ibn Khalaf and Ubayy ibn Khalaf in exchange for a striped cloak and ten ounces (of silver), and he freed him for the sake of Allah. So Allah revealed: "﴿By the night when it covers﴾" up to His saying: "﴿Indeed, your efforts are diverse﴾," (referring to) the efforts of Abu Bakr, Umayya, and Ubayy; up to His saying: "﴿and denied the best﴾," he said: "(That is) la ilaha illa Allah." Up to His saying: "﴿We will ease him toward difficulty﴾," he said: "The Fire."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: "﴿As for he who gives and fears (Allah)﴾," (the giving is) of wealth, "and fears (Allah)," he said: "fears his Lord." "﴿and believes in the best﴾," he said: "believes in the replacement from Allah." "﴿We will ease him toward ease﴾," he said: "toward the good from Allah." "﴿And as for he who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient﴾," he said: "He withholds his wealth and considers himself independent of his Lord." "﴿and denies the best﴾," he said: "(denies) the replacement from Allah." "﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾," he said: "toward evil from Allah."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him regarding "and believes in the best," he said: "He is certain of the replacement."

Ibn Jarir also narrated from him regarding "﴿and believes in the best﴾," he said: "He affirms la ilaha illa Allah." "﴿And as for he who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient﴾," he said: "He whom Allah has made wealthy, yet he withholds the zakat."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from ʿAmir ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: Abu Bakr used to free (slaves) for (embracing) Islam in Makkah, and he would free old women and women when they embraced Islam. His father said to him: "O my son, I see you freeing weak people. If only you would free strong men who would stand with you, protect you, and defend you." He said: "O father, I only desire what is with Allah." He said: "(p-1631) One of the people of my household told me that this verse was revealed concerning him: ﴿As for he who gives and fears, and believes in the best, We will ease him toward ease.﴾"

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: "﴿As for he who gives and fears, and believes in the best﴾," he said: (this refers to) Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. "﴿And as for he who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient, and denies the best﴾," he said: (this refers to) Abu Sufyan ibn Harb.

al-Bukhari, Muslim, the authors of the Sunan, and others narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) at a funeral, and he said: 'There is none among you but that his place in Paradise and his place in the Fire have been written.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall we not rely (on that)?' He said: 'Act, for each is made easy for what he was created for. As for the one who is among the people of happiness, he will be made easy for the deeds of the people of happiness; and as for the one who is among the people of wretchedness, he will be made easy for the deeds of the people of wretchedness.' Then he recited: ﴿As for he who gives and fears, and believes in the best﴾ up to His saying 'for hardship.'"

Ahmad, Muslim, and others narrated from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah that Suraqah ibn Malik said: "O Messenger of Allah, in what should we act? In a matter for which the decrees have been settled and the pens have run, or in a matter in which action is yet to be undertaken?" He said: "Rather, in a matter for which the decrees have been settled and the pens have run." Suraqah said: "Then why act, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Act, for each is made easy for what he was created for." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then recited this verse: ﴿As for he who gives and fears﴾ up to His saying ﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾ (32).

The hadith of ʿImran ibn Husayn has already been mentioned in the surah before this one, and there are hadiths on this matter through a group of the Companions.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "You will all surely enter Paradise except he who refuses." They said: "And who would refuse to enter Paradise?" Then he recited: ﴿He who denied and turned away﴾.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: "No one of this Ummah will remain but that Allah will admit him into Paradise, except one who runs away from Allah as a bad camel runs away from its owners. Whoever does not believe me, then Allah says: ﴿None will burn therein except the most wretched, who denied and turned away﴾," (meaning) he denied what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought and turned away from it.

Ahmad, al-Hakim, and al-Diya' narrated from Abu Umamah al-Bahili that he was asked about the gentlest word he had heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Surely all of you will be admitted by Allah into Paradise, except one who runs away from Allah as a camel runs away from its owners.'"

Ahmad, Ibn Majah, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "None enters the Fire except the wretched." It was said: "And who is the wretched?" He said: "The one who does not perform any obedience to Allah and does not abandon any disobedience to Allah."

Ahmad and al-Bukhari narrated from him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "All of my Ummah will enter Paradise on the Day of Resurrection except one who refuses." They said: "And who would refuse, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Whoever obeys me enters Paradise, and whoever disobeys me has refused."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿUrwah that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq freed seven, all of whom were tortured for the sake of Allah: Bilal, ʿAmir ibn Fuhayrah, al-Nahdiyyah and her daughter, Zinnirah, Umm ʿAys, and the slave woman of Banu al-Muammil. Concerning him was revealed: ﴿And the most righteous will be kept away from it﴾ up to the end of the surah.

al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from ʿAmir ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr what we mentioned earlier from him, with an addition: concerning him this verse was revealed: ﴿As for he who gives and fears, up to His saying: ﴿and no one has with him any favor to be repaid, except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High. And he will surely be satisfied.﴾

al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from him something similar through another chain.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And the most righteous will be kept away from it﴾, that he said: "He is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq."

This surah is Meccan according to the majority, though it has been said to be Madinan.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The surah of *By the night when it covers* was revealed in Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted the like of this from Ibn al-Zubayr.

al-Bayhaqi transmitted in his *Sunan* from Jabir ibn Samurah that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ and similar surahs in the Zuhr and 'Asr prayers."

al-Tabarani transmitted in *al-Awsat* from Anas that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led them in the midday prayer (al-hajirah), raised his voice, and recited ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ and ﴿By the night when it covers﴾. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, were you commanded in this prayer with something?' He said: 'No, but I wanted to set the time for you.'" The hadith "Why did you not pray with *Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High*, and *By the sun and its brightness*, and *By the night when it covers*" has already been mentioned.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "I say that this surah was revealed concerning generosity and miserliness: ﴿By the night when it covers﴾."

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.**

(p-1629) His saying ﴿By the night when it covers﴾: that is, it veils with its darkness what was luminous.

al-Zajjaj said: the night covers the horizon and everything between the heaven and the earth, so the light of the day departs. It was said that it covers the day, and it was said that it covers the earth. The first is preferable.

﴿And by the day when it displays itself﴾: that is, it appears, becomes clear and manifest, because the darkness that was in the night has been removed, and this happens with the rising of the sun.

﴿And by He who created the male and the female﴾: here *ma* (ما) is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*), meaning "and by He who (*alladhi*) created the male and the female."
